title: Fats & Oils
subtitle: 8000–1200 BC · Fat Before Oil: Rendered Fat, the First Butter, the Olive of the Levant and the Sesame of the Indus

entries.label: Ebla’s inspectors check the olive growers and millers
entries.hint: Crime has been part of the oil trade for some 5,000 years, Mueller says: the earliest known documents to mention olive oil, cuneiform tablets from Ebla of the twenty-fourth century BC, refer to teams of inspectors who checked olive growers and millers for fraudulent practices.
entries.note: UNVERIFIED (popular history; tablets not read): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), ch.1. The claim is attractive to a writer on olive-oil fraud and has not been checked against the Ebla editions; compare fats-1750-1850 and fats-1960-today on later fraud rules.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The oldest recipes: fat in the pot

entries.label: The Yale culinary tablets: fat goes into the pot after water
entries.hint: Three Old Babylonian tablets in the Yale collection, the oldest known recipes, build almost every dish the same way: put water in the pot, then add ‘some fat’ (lipa, in Sumerian i-udu, ‘sheep fat’), then the aromatics. The cooked broth becomes a fatty ‘pot fat’ that is served or reused as a cooking liquid; grain, too, is cooked in fatty broth.
entries.note: ANCHOR (translation and commentary read): Bottéro, The Oldest Cuisine in the World (2004; Chicago 2011 ed.), the tablets dated ‘around 1600 BCE’ (PDF p.17), the fat and ‘pot fat’ discussion on printed pp.67–68 (PDF pp.80–81) and the fatty broth for grain on printed p.71 (PDF p.84). The sheep-fat reading rests on the Sumerian i-udu as Bottéro explains it.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Akkadian oil-plant and the sesame identification

entries.label: Where the herds were missing: the tsetse belt and the Americas lean on tree fats
entries.loc: Africa south of the Sahara and the Americas
entries.hint: Kiple’s editors sketch how goats and sheep, then pigs, cattle, water buffalo, horses and camels were domesticated across the core of the Old World, and exploited for milk, hides, labour and meat once they were. On the periphery that range was missing: in Africa south of the Sahara, trypanosomal infection delivered by the tsetse fly often discouraged livestock keeping, and in the New World, apart from dogs, turkeys and llamas and their relatives, there was relatively little animal domestication. For many people, they say, this meant an absence of animal fats in the diet, which nature remedied to some extent by the fat in avocados for many Americans and by palm oil and coconut palms for most of the tropical world.
entries.note: CONTEXT (book read): Kiple & Ornelas, eds., The Cambridge World History of Food (2000), introduction to Part II, PDF p.110. This is the editors’ general overview, not a site-based finding, and ‘an absence of animal fats’ is their phrase for many people, not all: the folio’s own entries show exceptions in the Sahara (ec10) and among hunters (fats-130000bc-8000bc::ec9, ec10). The Pacific and the Americas’ dogs, turkeys and llamas are not worked out here.

entries.label: The secondary-products revolution: when did people begin to milk?
entries.hint: Sherratt argues that domestic animals were first kept largely for meat and only some millennia later for milk, wool and traction, so milking cannot be assumed from the start of domestication. The first picture of milking is Uruk, in the fourth millennium BC, but the ages at which Swiss Neolithic cattle were killed (Pfyn and Cortaillod, 3800–3500 BC) and at Eschen-Lutzengüetle (about 4000 BC) show mostly adult females, which makes milking likely in Europe by 4000 BC. He adds that sheep were regularly used as milk animals in northern Europe until the Industrial Revolution.
entries.note: ANCHOR (paper read): Sherratt, ‘The Secondary Exploitation of Animals in the Old World’, World Archaeology 15 (1983), the section ‘The antiquity of dairying’. The argument is his hypothesis from kill-off patterns; the direct chemical evidence came later (Dudd & Evershed 1998, read for its method).

entries.label: Sesame, peanuts and broad beans in a Chekiang Neolithic layer: a find few believe
entries.hint: Remains of peanuts have been reported from Lungshanoid sites in Chekiang and Kiangsi, from layers radiocarbon dated to the third millennium BC. The peanut is thought to be a South American plant that reached China only in the sixteenth century, and scholars are sceptical: sesame and broad beans were reported from the same layer, and these also are thought to have arrived in China much later. Anderson calls the claims for these seeds at one famous site highly irresponsible. The find, if real, would put an oil seed in China two thousand years before sesame is said to come with the Han; most take it as a mix-up of layers or identifications.
entries.note: CONTESTED (identification and context): Chang (1977), ‘Ancient China’, p.27 (PDF p.36), citing Chechiang Sheng 1960 and Ho 1969, An 1972; Anderson, The Food of China (1988) PDF p.26. The closing sentence is the folio’s summary of the scholars’ doubt. Bray (SCC 6.2, 1984, PDF p.275) states that there can be no doubt that the peanut reached China from America after Columbus, probably via the Portuguese to Fukien early in the sixteenth century, while noting the supposed Neolithic peanuts that have led some to postulate a Chinese origin. Compare ec12 for the Peruvian peanut and fats-1500-1750::x2 for the sixteenth-century arrival.

entries.label: Was the Indus cow milked? Fuller’s caution
entries.hint: Fuller notes that archaeologists often assume domestic cattle mean milk, but cattle are not universally milked and some groups in India today abstain from it entirely, so dairying is a product of particular cultural histories. For the Harappans, milk use has been argued from perforated pots and from the ages at which cattle and buffalo were killed, but the evidence is inferential. His working synthesis has the Mehrgarh package of the seventh millennium BC — goats, wheat, barley, perhaps pulses and linseed — arrive from the west, with zebu cattle, cotton and eventually sesame domesticated in the region and forming the base of Harappan urbanism.
entries.note: ANCHOR (paper read): Fuller, ‘Agricultural Origins and Frontiers in South Asia: A Working Synthesis’, Journal of World Prehistory 20 (2006) pp.1–86 (PDF pp.14–15, 22 and 28). Compare ec17 for the lipid result and ec4 for sesame at Harappa.

entries.label: The Akkadian ‘oil-plant’ šamaššammū: sesame, or flax?
entries.hint: Cuneiform texts from about 2400 BC name an oil plant, Akkadian šamaššammū, whose identity was disputed for decades. Dorothea Bedigian and others argue that it is sesame; the Chicago Assyrian Dictionary translated it ‘flax’ while printing texts that favour sesame. An Old Babylonian text about crushing 90 gur of it before the autumn rains shows a summer crop harvested in the fall, which fits sesame.
entries.note: CONTESTED (identification): Bedigian (ed.), Sesame: The Genus Sesamum (2011) ch.1 printed p.4 (PDF p.29) — the 2400 BC attestation, the Chicago Assyrian Dictionary ‘Š’ volume (1989) giving ‘flax’, the Dossin 1933 text on 90 gur, the Sumerian ilu/Akkadian ellu against Dravidian el/ellu. Bedigian is the chief proponent of the sesame reading, so the sesame identification should be read as her case, endorsed by Fuller and Zohary & Hopf.

entries.label: Egypt’s best oil, nhh: sesame, castor, or something else?
entries.hint: From the nineteenth dynasty (1320–1200 BC) Egyptian texts name a highest-quality oil, nhh, whose identity is a mystery: some authors made it castor oil, a view disputed because castor oil is unpalatable and toxic; the Egyptian word ake has been proposed for sesame. Sesame was in Egypt but as a prize rather than a farm crop: baskets of sesame seeds lay in Tutankhamun’s tomb (c.1325 BC), which Zohary and colleagues read as a rare import fit for the king’s table, not local cultivation.
entries.note: CONTESTED (identification): Kiple (2000) the sesame chapter p.414 (PDF p.451), citing Loret 1892 and Keimer 1924; Zohary, Hopf & Weiss, Domestication of Plants in the Old World (2012) PDF p.130, citing de Vartavan et al. 2010. Compare th1 for the same problem in Akkadian.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Butter, the olive, flax, sesame, mustard, palm fat and Crete’s oil

entries.label: Neolithic herders make the first butter
entries.hint: Once Neolithic people kept milking sheep and goats — domestic sheep and goats are in Iran from as early as 9000 BC — dairy products followed, and butter with them. The earliest butters came from the milk of sheep, goats and yak, not cattle, and the first butter was unintended. Where and when it was first made is still debated.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; the archaeology not read): Khosrova, Butter: A Rich History (2016) pp.25–27 (printed; PDF pp.46–48) — butter arrived with the Neolithic domestication of ruminants, sheep, goat and yak before cattle, with the origin ‘a subject of ongoing debate’. The residue evidence for early dairying (Evershed and colleagues, lipid analysis of Neolithic pottery) is in the research literature, not in the library, and is not cited here.

entries.label: Flax: an early oil and fibre crop
entries.hint: Flax is one of the first-wave founder crops of South-west Asia and the best-documented early oil and fibre plant. The seed holds about 40 per cent oil: in peasant communities linseed gave an edible oil and a high-grade lighting oil, cold pressing giving cooking oil and hot pressing a drying oil used for paints and varnishes. The date is the start of the folio, standing for the crop’s earliest use.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Zohary, Hopf & Weiss (2012) PDF pp.117–118 — flax as ‘apparently the earliest and the best-documented oil and fibre crop’, a first-wave founder crop, 40 per cent oil, lighting and edible oil in peasant communities, drying oil by hot pressing. Exact dating of oil use is not given there, so the date is the folio’s opening.

entries.label: Brassica and mustard seed: cakes at Jerf el Ahmar and weeds pressed for oil in Swiss lake villages
entries.loc: Jerf el Ahmar, Syria, Khafadje, Iraq and the Swiss lakes
entries.hint: Zohary and Hopf note that several cruciferous oil plants, radish, turnip, rape and the white, black and brown mustards, were amply recorded as oil or mustard sources in classical times, yet there are almost no archaeological records of their cultivation. Two cakes with crushed seed of Brassica or Sinapis were found by Willcox at Pre-Pottery Neolithic A Jerf el Ahmar in Syria, dated to the tenth millennium BP; many carbonised seeds were found about 5,000 years ago at the Temple Oval at Khafadje in Iraq, which Schiemann assigned to Brassica or Sinapis, two genera hard to tell apart when charred. In Switzerland, turnip seed in late Neolithic and Bronze Age lake-shore sites suggests it was an oil-bearing tolerated weed, and the authors say it is very likely that wild Brassica, Sinapis, Camelina and Descurainia seed was collected or even grown for oil in Switzerland and Germany in the late Neolithic. By Hellenistic and Roman times these crucifers were well-established oil crops, so the authors assume cultivation began earlier.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Zohary, Hopf & Weiss, Domestication of Plants in the Old World (4th ed., 2012), PDF p.129 (printed p.112), citing Willcox (2002), Bedigian & Harlan (1986), Schiemann (1933), Villaret-von Rochow (1967) and Schlichtherle (1981). The dates are the book’s; ‘tenth millennium BP’ is rendered here as about 8000 BC, and the use of the cakes and seeds for oil is the authors’ inference. Compare ec24 for the Chinese Banpo brassica seeds.

entries.label: Beeswax in Neolithic pots from about 7000 BC
entries.loc: Çayönü Tepesi and other early farming sites, Turkey
entries.hint: A study of lipid residues in about 6,400 pottery vessels from more than 150 Old World sites found beeswax in some 80 of them; the earliest sherds belong to the seventh millennium BC and come from several sites in what is now Turkey, among them Çayönü Tepesi, where the wax was exceptionally well preserved. The residues show that early farmers used the products of the honeybee, but not necessarily beekeeping: they may have taken wild honey and wax. Wax is a wax, not a fat, and is here for what it later does: it lights candles, seals pots and lubricates.
entries.note: SECONDARY (abstracts and news found by web search; the paper not read): Roffet-Salque et al., ‘Widespread exploitation of the honeybee by early Neolithic farmers’, Nature 527 (2015) pp.226–230. The closing clause about candles, seals and lubricants is the folio’s reading of why wax belongs in an atlas of fats.

entries.label: The opium poppy, a western Mediterranean crop with an oil seed, from La Marmotta to the Alpine lake villages
entries.loc: La Marmotta, Italy, and Neolithic and Bronze Age Europe
entries.hint: Zohary and Hopf write that the opium poppy is grown both for the latex of its unripe capsules and for its seeds, which are eaten as they are or pressed for poppy oil, used for eating and for industry; two series of cultivars have evolved, the opium forms and the oil varieties. Abundant waterlogged seeds of the domesticated plant come from Early Neolithic La Marmotta in Italy, about 7,750–7,150 cal BP, and carbonised seeds from the Linearbandkeramik settlements of Germany and Poland, from middle Neolithic France, and from Late Neolithic and Bronze Age lake-shore settlements in Switzerland, south Germany and north Italy. Poppies are missing from Neolithic sites in south-east Europe and south-west Asia and appear in Bronze Age Greece, Bulgaria and the former Yugoslavia, which together with the range of the wild setigerum poppy suggests a west Mediterranean domestication, a ‘second circle’ crop outside the Fertile Crescent.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Zohary, Hopf & Weiss, Domestication of Plants in the Old World (4th ed., 2012), PDF pp.126–128 (printed pp.109–111), citing Rottoli (1993, 2002), Kreuz (2007), van Zeist (1980) and Bakels (1982). The sites show the seed, not pressed oil; the oil use is the book’s description of the crop. Compare ec25 for Europe’s other northern oil seed.

entries.label: El Gigante: the avocado managed, then selected for bigger, thicker-skinned fruit
entries.hint: In the rockshelter of El Gigante, 1,725 avocado remains, mostly rind, and 79 whole or part seeds, with 56 of them directly radiocarbon dated within a sequence of 292 dates, show long-term management of the tree: human-directed selection for larger fruits with thicker rinds is evident as early as 7,565 to 7,265 years ago, and the change culminated by 2,250 to 2,080 years ago. Thick rinds protect the fruit from damage, let it hang longer on the tree and make the flesh easier to scoop out. Tree fruits, avocados among them, appear at the start of the sequence about 11,000 years ago, and maize begins to dominate the plant remains only after 4,400 years ago, so tree cultivation came before heavy reliance on a staple grain, the reverse of Asia.
entries.note: ANCHOR (article read): VanDerwarker et al., PNAS 122 (2025) e2417072122, abstract and §§ on the El Gigante assemblage and morphometrics (PDF pp.1–5). The article is about domestication, not fat; the avocado’s place among fat sources is Kiple’s (see fats-130000bc-8000bc::ec10).

entries.label: Dairy fat in Saharan pots: Takarkori, Libya
entries.hint: Lipid analysis of potsherds from the Takarkori rock shelter in the Libyan Sahara found milk fat absorbed in the pots, evidence of dairying by herders in the fifth millennium BC, when the Sahara was green. The analysis could not tell butter from cheese or yoghurt, only that milk was being heated and processed in pots; the same pots also held animal flesh fats and some plant oils. Kiple adds that Saharan cave paintings of cattle and deep wells dated to the ninth millennium BC point to early cattle-keeping for milk and blood.
entries.note: SECONDARY (the paper’s abstract and press coverage found by web search; the full paper not read): Dunne et al., ‘First dairying in green Saharan Africa in the fifth millennium bc’, Nature 486 (2012) pp.390–394; Kiple (2000) the cattle chapter p.492 (PDF p.529; Simoons 1971 on the Algerian paintings, Close & Wendorf 1992 on the eastern Sahara). The ‘7,000 years ago’ in press reports is the same fifth-millennium date.

entries.label: China’s pigs and dogs: meat and fat from Yangshao to Shang, and no milk
entries.hint: Chang writes that animals gave the ancient Chinese meat and fat, as well as bones, antlers, skins and feathers, but milk and milk products were apparently not used. Dogs and pigs have the longest histories among the domestic animals, found in large quantities at the Neolithic Yangshao and Lungshan sites and at all Shang and Zhou sites, and were the principal sources of meat; cattle, sheep and goats appear at some Yangshao sites but were probably not fully domesticated until the Lungshan period. At Anyang the bones of sheep, cattle and water buffalo come mostly from sacrificial burials, so beef and mutton were used in ritual and eaten outside it, he thinks, less commonly than pork.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read, OCR of a scanned copy): K. C. Chang, ‘Ancient China’, in Chang (ed.), Food in Chinese Culture (1977) p.29 (PDF p.38), citing Teilhard de Chardin & Young 1936 and Shih 1953. The fat is implied by ‘meat and fat’; Chang does not describe the fat’s use, and the 5000 BC start is the folio’s bracket for the Yangshao.

entries.label: The olive is domesticated in the Chalcolithic Levant
entries.loc: Jordan Valley and the Dead Sea region
entries.hint: Definite signs of olive domestication come from Chalcolithic sites in Israel and Jordan: charred olive stones and olive wood from Tuleilat Ghassul, dated about 6,800–5,800 years ago. Wild olive stones occur at earlier sites, but those do not show cultivation. The tree takes five or six years to bear and can fruit for centuries; charred stones show the tree and the fruit, not proof of oil.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read; PDF pages): Zohary, Hopf & Weiss, Domestication of Plants in the Old World, 4th ed. (2012) PDF pp.22, 133–137 — olive and date palm domestication ‘about 6,800–6,300 cal BP’ in the Chalcolithic Levant, the Tuleilat Ghassul stones at ca. 6,800–5,800 cal BP, earlier wild-olive finds at Nahal Oren and Grotta dell’Uzzo; Kiple, Cambridge World History of Food (2000) II.E.1 p.377 (‘5,000 or 6,000 years ago’, after Chandler 1950). Stones and wood date the tree, not the pressing: see te2 and ec8 for oil.

entries.label: Brassica seeds at Banpo: oil, or only greens?
entries.hint: At the early Neolithic village of Banpo in Shaanxi, remains of seeds have been identified with the genus Brassica, though several different species of vegetable are possible. Bray notes that these may have been used for oil, which would make the brassicas, with hemp, the likeliest of China’s first oil crops; but even Han archaeology says nothing of how oil was made, and the Chinese wedge press is not described before the Sung, though it is so simple that it may be very ancient. Simpler ways of getting oil, boiling the seed or pounding it in a mortar, were used in ancient Egypt and could go back far in China too.
entries.note: CONTEXT (books read): Chang (ed.), Food in Chinese Culture (1977) p.29 (PDF p.38, citing Shih et al. 1963); Bray, Agriculture, SCC vol. 6 part 2 (1984), ‘Oil crops’, PDF p.275, a conjecture of hers. The 4800–3600 BC bracket for the Yangshao village is supplied from general knowledge.

entries.label: Baltic pots go on cooking marine and freshwater food after farming arrives
entries.loc: The western Baltic: Denmark and northern Germany
entries.hint: A lipid study of 133 vessels and 100 charred residues from the western Baltic, from around the time domesticated plants and animals first arrived, found that about one vessel in five with preserved lipids was still used for marine and freshwater foods. The authors conclude that the new pottery was not used only for farm products and that economies were not wholly transformed when farming came; a larger dataset of 667 analyses from 528 vessels across the circum-Baltic hunter-gatherer sites, including the Ertebølle culture, extends the method. Fish, seal and shellfish fat stayed in the pot.
entries.note: SECONDARY (abstracts found by web search; papers not read): Craig et al., Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2011), on the western Baltic; a larger circum-Baltic dataset (PMC7211838, authors not confirmed here). The date is a placeholder for ‘the arrival of domesticates’; the closing clause is the folio’s paraphrase, since the abstracts name marine and freshwater foods, not specific fats.

entries.label: Ben, balanos and castor: the oils Egypt grew
entries.hint: Lucas lists the oils Egypt produced: ben oil, pressed from the nuts of the moringa tree that grows there and is probably indigenous, sweet, odourless and slow to turn rancid, so prized for cosmetics, for extracting flower perfumes and for cooking; balanos oil from the kernels of Balanites aegyptiaca, a tree once abundant whose fruit stones, several hundred of them, turn up in Twelfth Dynasty finds; castor oil, whose seeds appear in graves from the Badarian period; lettuce-seed oil for salad and cooking; and colocynth. Linseed oil is first recorded in the Ptolemaic period, and Lucas thinks it was used for cooking and lamps. The identity of the Egyptian names for many oils remains unknown.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read, OCR of a scanned copy): Lucas (1962) ch.XIII, PDF pp.395–400. The 4000–1800 BC bracket runs from the Badarian castor seeds to the Twelfth Dynasty balanos stones; Lucas gives the period names, not the years. Compare th2 for nhh, whose identification he does not settle.

entries.label: Canarium almond, coconut and candlenut in the waterlogged sites of Near Oceania
entries.loc: The Ramu valley and Kumbun Island, Papua New Guinea
entries.hint: Waterlogged sites in Near Oceania preserved the fruits, seeds and nuts of tree crops. A deposit by an ancient inland sea in the Ramu valley, radiocarbon dated to about 5,700–5,800 years ago, held Canarium almond, coconut, candlenut (Aleurites), Pangium and others; at Apalo on Kumbun Island off New Britain a deposit of 2300–2100 BC, earlier than the Lapita period, held Canarium indicum, coconut, Aleurites and more. Kirch reads this as the strongest evidence that the lowland peoples of Near Oceania had taken significant steps towards domesticating tree crops by the middle Holocene. The sources say nothing about pressing oil: these are fat-bearing nuts, grown and gathered.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (rev. ed.), ch.3, PDF p.93, citing Swadling, Araho & Ivuyo 1991 and Spriggs 1997. The ‘fat-bearing’ clause is the folio’s, as at ec5 of the pre-8000 BC folio.

entries.label: Palm fat in a tomb at Abydos? A claim the Egyptologist rejects
entries.hint: A tomb at Abydos dated to about 3000 BC yielded several kilograms of fat in the shape of its vessel; a chemical analysis of 1897 found mainly palmitic acid and glycerol and identified it as palm oil, and two modern books treat this as evidence that palm oil from Africa reached Egypt by 3000 BC. Lucas, the standard authority on Egyptian materials, called such identifications demonstrably wrong: palmitic acid is a constituent of most animal and vegetable fats, and the rancid-coconut smell of old tomb fats comes from a small proportion of nonanoic acid formed by decay. The tomb fats he and later analysts could identify were largely animal fats. The African oil palm may well be old (ec11); the Abydos jar does not show it.
entries.note: CONTESTED (identification): Kiple (2000) II.E.3 p.397 (PDF p.434), citing Friedel 1897 (Comptes Rendus 24: 648–51); Zuckerman, Planet Palm (2021) cites ‘archaeological findings’ for Egyptian palm-oil trade ‘as early as 3,000 B.C.’; against them Lucas, Ancient Egyptian Materials and Industries (4th ed., 1962) ch.XIII ‘Oils, fats and waxes’, PDF pp.393–395 (OCR of a scanned copy), including Banks & Hilditch’s analyses of tomb fats.

entries.label: Oil-palm nuts at West and Central African sites from about 3000 BC
entries.hint: The oil palm is native to Africa: Lynn notes fossil pollen of the palm in Niger Delta layers of the Miocene and that the South American palm is post-Columbian, with local names derived from West African ones. An abstract of a botanical study reports charred oil-palm shells (endocarps) in many archaeological sites in the rain-forest and woodland-savanna zones of West and Central Africa from about 5000 years ago, which would make the tree part of the region’s subsistence long before any written record.
entries.note: UNVERIFIED (one abstract seen through a web search; author and title not confirmed here — Vegetation History and Archaeobotany, DOI 10.1007/BF02342720): the ‘about 5000 BP’ endocarp finds. SECONDARY: Lynn, Commerce and Economic Change in West Africa (1997) p.1 (PDF p.21) for the African origin, citing archaeological evidence of Egyptian palm-oil trade in the third millennium BC (see ec7).

entries.label: Egypt’s “butter” is butter fat: ox fat, goose fat, and cheese in a First Dynasty jar
entries.hint: The Egyptians kept cows, sheep and goats and knew their fats, including milk fat. The records name butter (Twentieth Dynasty), ox fat (Eighteenth), white fat, once for cakes (Twentieth), and goose fat (New Kingdom and Twentieth). Lucas insists that the word translated ‘butter’ means butter fat, melted and settled to remove water and casein, which is the modern Egyptian samn and the Indian ghee, used for eating with food and cooking and never spread on bread; in a hot country the separation of butter fat is natural and unavoidable. The contents of two alabaster jars of First Dynasty date at Saqqara have recently been shown to be cheese. Papyri prescribe the fats of the gazelle, hippopotamus, crocodile, lion, cat and goat as hair ointments.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read, OCR of a scanned copy): Lucas, Ancient Egyptian Materials and Industries (4th ed., 1962), ch.XIII, ‘Animal fats’, PDF pp.397–398 (citing the Hearst and Ebers Papyri and the Saqqara cheese). Egypt is filed under the Near East in the atlas. Lucas is old: the First Dynasty cheese and the translations are as he reported them.

entries.label: Gold of pleasure: Camelina, the weed of flax that became northern Europe’s oil crop
entries.loc: Switzerland, Poland, Hungary, Germany and northern Italy
entries.hint: Zohary and Hopf call Camelina sativa, gold of pleasure or false flax, a relic oil plant that was an important oil crop in eastern and central Europe until the 1940s; the cultivated seeds hold 27 to 31 per cent edible oil. Its seeds appear repeatedly in central and eastern European archaeological sites, but late: the oldest come from the final Neolithic lake village of Auvernier in Switzerland, followed by Bronze Age finds of 1800–1200 BC from Poland, Hungary, Germany and north Italy, and Iron Age finds are more numerous, especially on the Baltic and North Sea coasts. In Anatolia the weed turns up among flax at Kuruçay, and a Late Bronze Age concentration at Hadidi on the Syrian–Turkish border suggests cultivation. The authors read the combined evidence as a secondary crop: the plant first became a weed of flax and cereals, and only later was picked up as an oil crop.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Zohary, Hopf & Weiss, Domestication of Plants in the Old World (4th ed., 2012), PDF p.128 (printed p.111), citing Schultze-Motel (1979), Kroll (1991), Wasylikowa et al. (2001) and Miller (1991). The book gives Auvernier as ‘ca 4,000 BC’ yet describes the earliest finds as of the fifth and fourth millennia BP, which would be 3000–1000 BC, so the folio’s bracket starts at 3000 BC; seeds show the plant, not pressing. Compare ec3 for flax and w1 for the cool north’s fats.

entries.label: The soybean is domesticated in north-east China: 2700 BC or 1000 BC?
entries.hint: The soybean, today’s leading oilseed, is a Chinese domesticate, but its date is contested. Legend and one authority put its cultivation at about 4,500 years, near 2700 BC, and a tradition in the Book of Odes places it in the 15th century BC; another reading, Trager’s, has the crop brought into China only around 1000 BC, and Needham dates its domestication to about 1000 BC, the start of the Zhou. The oil became important far later: for most of Chinese history the soybean was eaten as bean curd, sauce and meal.
entries.note: CONTESTED (dating): Kiple (2000) II.E.5 p.422 (PDF p.459; 4,500 years against ‘only around 1000 B.C.’ per Trager 1995; the Book of Odes tradition); Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) p.40 (PDF p.68) for about 1000 BC. Treat the dates as unsettled. The last sentence is the folio’s summary of the later oil history, not a claim from these pages.

entries.label: Sesame is a crop of the Harappan Indus
entries.hint: A lump of charred sesame was found at Harappa in Mature Harappan levels (2600/2500–2000 BC), and sesame turns up in the second half of the 2000s BC at Miri Qalat in Makran. Fuller’s review of finds from 22 sites concludes that cultivated sesame was an established crop in north-western South Asia by Harappan times. The Harappan word tila became the Indian word for all oil (tel).
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Bedigian (ed.), Sesame: The Genus Sesamum (2011) ch.1 pp.3–4 (PDF pp.28–29) — Harappa (Vats 1940), Miri Qalat (Tengberg 1999), Fuller’s review (2003) of 22 sites, tila → tel; Achaya, Indian Food Tradition (1994) p.17 (the ‘lump of charred sesame’ at about two metres’ depth at Harappa; carbonised rāi, Brassica juncea, at Chanhudaro). Bedigian cautions that charring destroys sesame seed, so finds undercount it. Kiple (2000) II.E.4 p.412 gives Vats’s original date for the Harappa sesame as 3500–3050 BC and calls it ‘probably much too early’ (pre-radiocarbon).

entries.label: Mustard and linseed at the Harappan sites; animal fats by boiling
entries.hint: Carbonised mustard seed (rāi) was found at Chanhudaro, and linseed at Harappan sites. Achaya infers that knowledge of oilseeds implied knowledge of their oils, and that the fats of the many animals eaten were probably obtained simply by boiling.
entries.note: SECONDARY (inference marked by the author): Achaya (1994) pp.17–18 (PDF pp.35–36, OCR of a scanned PDF) — ‘knowledge of oilseeds implied, in all likelihood, knowledge of their oils’ and animal fats ‘probably also obtained easily enough, simply by boiling’. The oils themselves are not attested; the finds are seeds.

entries.label: Indus pots held mostly animal fat, with little sign of dairy
entries.loc: Haryana, north-west India, Rakhigarhi, Farmana, Masudpur
entries.hint: Lipid analysis of Mature Harappan pottery from urban and rural sites in north-west India found appreciable lipid in 71 per cent of the vessels, all of it degraded animal fat. Isotope values put about 60 per cent of the 73 vessels measured in the range of non-ruminant fats, though pigs are only 2–3 per cent of the bones and cattle dominate the animal remains; only four vessels, 5.5 per cent, fell in the dairy range, although the ages at which Harappan cattle were killed suggest that females were kept for milk. No aquatic biomarkers and no millet marker were found. The authors stress that the lack of local modern reference fats, and possible mixtures of plant and animal products, make the results hard to read.
entries.note: ANCHOR (paper read): Suryanarayan et al., ‘Lipid residues in pottery from the Indus Civilisation in northwest India’, Journal of Archaeological Science 125 (2021) 105291, abstract and §§3.2–4.1 (the cattle ages at Harappa are Miller 2004 as cited there). See th3 for the argument about milk.

entries.label: The olive in Egypt’s records: a sacred tree at Heliopolis, and oil from Syria
entries.hint: Olive trees, olives and olive oil are seldom named in Egypt’s hieroglyphic records. Lucas finds two references to a sacred olive tree at Heliopolis in the Pyramid Texts (Fifth and Sixth Dynasties); olive oil among spoil from Syria on a Fifth Dynasty fragment at Abusir; olive-lands in the Twentieth Dynasty; and an Eighteenth Dynasty mural showing a branch with olives. Reisner is quoted as saying olive oil was certainly imported from Palestine and Syria during the Fourth Dynasty. Of the classical writers, Strabo later found large olive trees only in the Fayum and said the oil had a disagreeable smell. The pharaoh’s olive groves for Ra’s lamps (fats-1200bc-300bc::b6) rest on this thin record.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read, OCR of a scanned copy): Lucas (1962) ch.XIII, ‘Olive oil’, PDF p.401. The dynasties are his; the 2600 BC start is the usual date of the Fourth Dynasty and is supplied from general knowledge. Compare ec9 and x4 for the Levantine oil that reached Egypt.

entries.label: Palace oil stores at Ebla, Mari, Ugarit and Minoan Crete
entries.hint: Olive oil was an important part of the royal treasuries of Ebla, Mari, Ugarit and Minoan Crete, kept in huge quantities in earthenware jars in the palace cellars. Cuneiform tablets at Ebla and Linear B tablets in Crete are said to describe broad olive plantations, large-scale mills and an extensive trade in oil.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; tablets not read): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011) ch.1 — ‘earnings from the sale of olive oil were already the lifeblood of several Mediterranean economies’ in the 2000s BC; the palace-cellar and tablet claims are his summary, not checked against the Ebla or Linear B editions. See ec8 and te2 for the better-sourced Cretan and Cypriot evidence.

entries.label: The sunflower is domesticated in eastern North America
entries.hint: The sunflower, now one of the world’s great oil crops, is a unique contribution of temperate North America: seeds from eastern North America show it domesticated before 1500 BC, and it was extensively cultivated there before 500 BC. Native Americans prized the seed as food and used other parts of the plant for a variety of purposes; it reached Europe in 1568 as a garden flower, and became an oil crop only later.
entries.note: SECONDARY (encyclopedia chapter): Kiple (2000) II.E.6 p.428 (PDF p.465) for the domestication before 1500 BC and wide cultivation before 500 BC; the 1568 arrival in Europe is fats-1500-1750::th2. Kiple does not say the early cultivators pressed the seed for oil, and the date range is the folio’s bracket round his two statements.

entries.label: Mesopotamian butter is always clarified
entries.hint: A daughter of the king Shu-Sin, setting out for a foreign land about the end of the 2000s BC, took butter, cheese, oil and fruit among her provisions. In that hot land butter (himētu) was always clarified: it was made from boiled milk and so did not turn rancid — the ancestor of the Indian ghee.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translations read in Bottéro): Bottéro, Oldest Cuisine (2011) printed pp.69–70 (PDF pp.82–83) — ‘butter was always clarified in that warm land, that is, made out of boiled milk, and therefore did not become rancid’; the provisions of Shu-Sin’s daughter near the end of the 2000s BC. The link with ghee is the folio’s observation, not Bottéro’s; ghee is attested in India from the Vedas (see fats-1200bc-300bc).

entries.label: Peanuts grown in Peru by 2000 BC
entries.hint: Evidence exists of peanuts grown in Peru as early as 2000 BC. The Americas had few fat animals: Kiple notes that, besides dogs, turkeys and llamas, there was relatively little animal domestication in the New World, which meant for many an absence of animal fats in the diet, partly remedied by the fat in avocados. The peanut would later become an oil crop in Africa, India and China.
entries.note: SECONDARY (encyclopedia chapters): Kiple (2000) the peanut chapter p.365 (PDF p.402), citing Sauer 1993; the introduction to Part II p.73 (PDF p.110) for the absence of animal fats. The Peruvian date rests on Sauer’s survey, not on a find described here.

entries.label: Crete grows rich on exported oil
entries.hint: In the last centuries of the Bronze Age, Crete was growing great numbers of olive trees and getting rich on the export of oil. Kiple’s account compares it with Greece, which two thousand years later would also learn the dangers of oil monoculture when war cut off trade.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Kiple (2000) II.E.1 p.377 (PDF p.414), citing Trager 1995 and Tannahill 1988 (both secondary; not read). The Linear B ‘wild olives’ reading is rejected by Foxhall, Olive Cultivation in Ancient Greece (2007) ch.1 §1.3. See te2 for the evidence of processing.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Rendering, the olive press and a claim about early soap

entries.label: Rendering: the oldest way to extract fat
entries.hint: The first method humans used to extract fat was ‘undoubtedly’ rendering: heating animal or fish tissue, dry or in water, until the fat separates. The quality of the earliest rendered fat must have been poor; later steam heating allowed high-quality rendering. The date is a placeholder at the folio’s start, since rendering must be far older than farming.
entries.note: CONTEXT: Kiple (2000) II.E.1 p.376 (PDF p.413) — ‘The first method humans employed to extract oils was undoubtedly rendering’, which the author does not date; the placement at c.8000 BC is only the folio’s baseline. Rendering of bone grease is in fact far older: see fats-130000bc-8000bc::te1 (Neumark-Nord, about 125,000 years ago).

entries.label: Blubber lamps of the Late Mesolithic north
entries.hint: Hunter-gatherers of the Late Mesolithic in northern Europe, the Ertebølle culture of Denmark, northern Germany and southern Sweden, used small lamps whose residues have been chemically analysed to show what they burned; the paper’s title names them blubber lamps. The same people made pottery well before farming reached them, so that light, heat and cooking in the far north ran on sea-mammal and fish fat.
entries.note: UNVERIFIED (only the title and context seen through a web search; the findings not read): Antiquity article ‘Illuminating the Late Mesolithic: residue analysis of blubber lamps from northern Europe’ (Cambridge Core; authors not confirmed here); the Ertebølle pottery context from a Springer article on Dutch Swifterbant pottery. The dates are the usual span of the Ertebølle culture, supplied from general knowledge, not read in these pages.

entries.label: Soap from fat and ash: an early Mesopotamian claim
entries.hint: Popular histories date the earliest soapmaking — boiling fat with wood-ash alkali — to Sumer and Babylonia about 2800–2500 BC, on the evidence of clay cylinders and tablets. This is a thin lead: it is not examined here, and the identification of the residue as soap is not tested.
entries.note: UNVERIFIED (thin lead): a frequently repeated claim in popular histories of soap; no source in the library supports it (Ward, The Clean Body, and the Unilever histories begin their accounts later). Included because soap is the longest-running non-food use of fats; treat the date and the object as unconfirmed. See fats-300bc-600ad for the sources that do attest soap.

entries.label: Cyprus and Crete press olives at scale
entries.hint: By the Late Bronze Age there is clear evidence for relatively large-scale olive processing on Cyprus and in Crete. The view that the palaces used only wild olives, based on a speculative reading of Linear B signs, is unlikely to be right. It is not clear whether olive technology spread from one centre or was invented more than once.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Foxhall, Olive Cultivation in Ancient Greece (2007) ch.1 §1.3 — Hadjisavvas (1992) for Cyprus, Hamilakis (1996, 1999) for Crete, and her own rejection of the ‘wild olives’ reading of Linear B (Foxhall 1995: 241–2). Page numbers not available in the extracted text; chapter and section cited.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Sesame to Mesopotamia and Egypt; two oil crops of the Americas and China

entries.label: Sesame travels from the Indus to Mesopotamia
entries.loc: The Indus valley to southern Mesopotamia
entries.hint: Sesame reached Mesopotamia in the Early Bronze Age, soon after its domestication in the Indus: seeds from Abu Salabikh date to the middle of the 2000s BC, and by 2000 BC it was a crop of great importance. The Sumerian and Akkadian names for the oil (ilu, ellu) are strikingly close to the early Dravidian names for sesame (el, ellu), and merchants moved it overland and by sea. Mesopotamia became the centre from which sesame spread to the Mediterranean.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read) + CONTESTED (linguistics): Bedigian (2011) ch.1 pp.4–5 (PDF pp.29–30) — Charles’s Abu Salabikh seeds, Late Bronze Age finds at Sabi Abyad and Tell Sheikh Hamad, the Sumerian/Akkadian/Dravidian name comparison (Bedigian 1985; Southworth 1995; Witzel 1999). Herodotus’s remark that Babylonian oil came only from sesame is quoted on p.5. Kiple (2000) II.E.4 p.413 says that ‘to date, no sesame seeds have been recovered from excavations in Mesopotamia’; Bedigian’s 2011 chapter cites the later Abu Salabikh finds (Charles 1993, 1994), which correct the older statement.

entries.label: Canaanite oil for Egypt; olives on the Uluburun ship
entries.loc: The southern Levant, Egypt and the Anatolian coast
entries.hint: Olive horticulture did not play a major role in Bronze Age Egypt, which instead imported oil from the southern Levant — a trade well documented in the Bronze Age archaeology; Cretan oil, Mueller adds, also went to Egypt for unguents, cosmetics and embalming. Thousands of olive stones, some 2,500 of them in a single Canaanite jar, came from the Late Bronze Age Uluburun shipwreck off the south-west Turkish coast, from the late 14th century BC, showing the oil trade by sea.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read) + SECONDARY: Zohary, Hopf & Weiss (2012) PDF pp.137–138 (Stager 1985; Kom el-Rabi’a and Tell el-Dab’a stones of the 18th–16th centuries BC; Haldane 1993 on Uluburun); Mueller (2011) ch.1 for the Cretan exports. Compare fats-1200bc-300bc::b6 on Egyptian olive groves.

entries.label: Sesame among the grave goods of Tutankhamun
entries.hint: By about 1500 BC sesame had reached Egypt: 60 ml of sesame seed, the main ingredient of one of the containers of food, drink, ointments, perfumes and oils in the ‘Annexe’ of King Tutankhamun’s tomb (reigned about 1332–1323 BC), is the only sesame ever recorded from ancient Egypt and the earliest from the Near East and Africa. Egypt had its own oils (see the Abydos palm fat, ec7); sesame joined them from the east.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Bedigian (2011) ch.1 p.5 (PDF p.30) and Kiple (2000) II.E.4 p.413 (PDF p.450; the 60 ml and the ‘Annexe’, from Christian de Vartavan’s examination of the Kew boxes; Kiple says ‘around 1350 B.C.’), citing Vartavan 1990. Date taken from the reign; not re-checked against Vartavan.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Climate and the northern/southern fat divide

entries.label: Climate sets the fat: animal fat in the north, plant oil in the south
entries.hint: Historically northern Europeans built diets on animal fat because their climate did not suit oilseed crops and their pastures raised animals easily, and Scandinavian fishing peoples ate marine fats; in the Mediterranean, Africa and Asia raising large herds was impractical and fats came mostly from plants such as olive trees and oil palms. A French scholar’s ‘two worlds’ — wine and oil in the east Mediterranean, beer, mead and animal fat beyond — puts the same divide in the archaic period. The date is a placeholder for this baseline.
entries.note: CONTEXT (framing sources read): Kiple (2000) II.E.1 pp.375–376 (PDF pp.412–413) — ‘historical differences in patterns of fat consumption largely resulted from environmental conditions’; Foxhall (2007) ch.1, citing Brun 2004a for the archaic divide between the ‘world of wine and oil’ and that of ‘beer, mead and animal fat’. The date is a placeholder; the divide is dated by neither source.
